title: Prep me for tomorrow's room
when: You have a meeting on the calendar and thirty minutes to get ready.
prompt: I'm meeting [names] from [company] tomorrow about [topic]. Tell me who they are, what has moved at their company recently, and every real connection between us.
why: Puts their public profile and company news next to your own history with them: places you both worked, people you both know, the last thing you talked about.

title: Prepare for a conference
when: You have an event tomorrow with hundreds of people and no plan.
prompt: Tomorrow is [event]. Find the partners, speakers and companies taking part, cross them with my network, and help me prepare. My goal is to meet [investors and founders].
why: Turns the speaker list into a ranked list of who to look for, who can introduce you, and what to say.

title: Prep me for a partner meeting
when: You're meeting another firm about investing together (co-investment), selling a company (exit), or buying one to add to a company you already own (add-on).
prompt: I'm meeting [names] from [firm] tomorrow about [co-investment / exit / add-on]. Tell me who they are, what has moved in their portfolio in the last quarter, which of their deals touched ours, and every real connection between us.
why: Puts the recent changes in their portfolio next to yours and finds the overlaps a search would never turn up.

title: Due diligence on a partner, with an honest view from people you know
when: A partnership is serious enough that you want to check it independently, before you sign a confidentiality agreement (NDA).
prompt: I'm evaluating a potential partnership with @[company]. Run due diligence: who runs it, who backs it, who their key partners and clients are, and any red flags. Then tell me who in my network is connected to any of those companies and who can give me a warm, honest read.
why: Maps the web of owners and board members around the company, then compares it with the people you know directly. It finds the person at a sister company that nobody would think to call.

title: Company diligence before investing
when: An investment is on the table and you need the full picture, and to know what is missing from it.
prompt: I'm evaluating an investment in @[company]. Run due diligence: who runs it, who backs it, who sits on the board, key customers and partners, and any governance red flags. Then tell me who in my network is connected to any of those people or companies and who can give me a candid, off-the-record read.
why: Lists what it could not confirm as things to check (for example, no public list of board members, or funding rounds reported differently in different places), and ranks who in your network can fill each gap.

title: A reference on the leadership before we invest
when: You're keeping the founder or CEO in their job and want an honest opinion of them.
prompt: We're about to back @[company] and keep @[person] in place. Map their career and every company behind it, then tell me who in my network overlapped with them and would give me an honest read on how they actually operate.
why: Maps their career, then finds the people who worked with them at each step and says what each one is best placed to tell you.

title: The honest reference before I hire
when: You're about to send a job offer.
prompt: I'm about to make an offer to @[person] for [role]. Map their career and the companies behind it, then tell me who in my network overlapped with them and who would give me a candid, off-the-record read.
why: Off-the-record references from your own network, found in minutes instead of over a week of asking around.

title: Who can actually introduce me to this investor
when: You're raising money and need people who can introduce you, not a list of funds.
prompt: I'm raising [round] for [thesis]. Find the funds that have backed comparable companies in the last 24 months, then rank who in my network can make a genuine warm introduction to each, and who I should not use.
why: Ranks each way in by how strong the relationships are, and tells you which contacts are too out of touch, or too far from the decision, to use.

title: Find your way into a fund
when: You want to reach a specific fund through people, not an email out of the blue.
prompt: Which companies has @[fund] invested in over the past three years? Do a deep research and find people in my network who have been part of those companies.
why: Turns the list of companies the fund has invested in into a list of people you already know there who can vouch for you.

title: Who can reach the partners at this firm
when: You know the firm. You need the right person there, and a way to reach them.
prompt: Who can reach the partners at @[firm]? First from shared work and investment history alone, then through my own network. Rank the paths and tell me which not to use.
why: Looks at public information first (people linked through past jobs, shared employers), then your own network, and gives you a list of paths not to use.

title: Reach co-investors and fund investors (LPs)
when: You're building a group of investors for a deal (a syndicate), or a relationship with a firm to invest alongside.
prompt: Who has co-invested alongside @[firm] in the last 36 months, and which of those funds is now raising or deploying in [sector]? Rank who in my network can make a genuine warm introduction to each, and who we should not use.
why: Finds the funds, checks what they are doing now, then ranks your ways in. It warns you when a match only has a similar name and is not a real match.

title: Find the right people in my network
when: You need a short list of people from your own connections who match a description.
prompt: Find people in my network with more than [3,000] LinkedIn connections whose role is about [relationship intelligence]: executives, managing directors, partners. Give me the top [20].
why: Sorts through your own network in seconds, using details LinkedIn does not let you search by.

title: Who in my network is relevant to what I am doing now
when: You're starting a new project, entering a new market, or facing a new problem.
prompt: I'm working on [what]. Who in my network is most relevant to it, and why? Think expertise, position, and who they know. Give me the top [10] with a reason for each.
why: Looks at the full picture of each person rather than their job title, so the right person shows up even when their profile headline does not say it.

title: Who left, and where did they go
when: You're keeping track of the people who leave a firm or company.
prompt: Track senior movement in and out of @[company] over the last 18 months. Who left, where did they go, and which of them is now reachable through my network?
why: Shows where former employees went, from public information, and which of them you can reach.

title: Review your week
when: Friday. You want to know what happened, who you met, and what carries over to next week.
prompt: It's the end of the week. Do a weekly review of my conversations, messages, email and calendar, and who I connected with, so I get a 360 view of new connections and what to keep top of mind for next week.
why: Reads all the places you talk to people and writes the review you would not have written yourself.

title: My network is going stale
when: Once a month, before losing touch costs you.
prompt: Show me the ten people in my network I should reconnect with this month, with a specific, non-generic reason for each based on what has changed on their side.
why: Each reason comes from what changed for them (a new role, money raised, a company sold), not from how long it has been since you spoke.

title: Work out the network of this company
when: You want to understand an organisation through the people who joined it and left it.
prompt: What is the inferred network of @[company]? Show me the alumni movement: where people came from, where they went, and which of them I can reach.
why: Shows the organisation as people coming and going over time, not as a chart of who reports to whom.

title: Summarise my network
when: You want a quick overview for yourself or a partner.
prompt: Create a summary of my network: the most influential people, where it is strong and where it is thin, and what I should do about it.
why: Sets out the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats in your relationships (a SWOT), with the names behind each finding.

title: What did we talk about last time
when: There's a name on your calendar you only half remember.
prompt: @[person] is on my calendar. What did we last talk about, what did I promise, and what has changed for them since?
why: Reads your own emails, messages and notes to find your history, then checks what has changed for them.

title: Prep for a customer call
when: A call with a possible customer or a design partner (an early customer who helps shape the product), and you want to know the people, not just the company.
prompt: I have a call with @[company] about [what]. Who is on their side, who decides, who in my network knows them, and what has the company said publicly about [topic] this year?
why: Maps the people involved in the buying decision and your ways to reach them, in one go.

title: Draft the follow-up
when: The meeting just ended.
prompt: I just met @[person]. Based on my notes and our history, draft a short follow-up in my tone that confirms [what we agreed] and proposes [next step].
why: Drafts it the way you write, using your own note on your tone, with the details of this relationship.

title: Map the sister companies
when: The company you're looking at is part of a complicated group of companies with shared owners.
prompt: Do a deep research behind @[company]: find all of their partner and sibling companies, the shared board members, and see who in my network works in any of them.
why: Finds the board members shared across the group, then the people you know inside it.

title: Who is this person, really
when: You've been sent a name and nothing else.
prompt: Who is @[person]? Career, companies, boards, what they have said publicly this year, and every connection between us. Flag anything I should know before I reply.
why: Their full profile and what you have in common, with anything awkward shown first.

title: What is a fund actually looking for
when: Before you pitch to them or invest alongside them.
prompt: What has @[fund] invested in over the last two years, at what stage and cheque size, and what does the pattern say they are looking for now? Who in my network has taken money from them?
why: Looks at the pattern in the deals they actually made, not at what their website says.

title: Who can introduce me to this person
when: You have a name and no way to reach them.
prompt: Who can introduce me to @[person]? Rank the paths by how well I know the connector and how well they know them, and tell me which one to use first.
why: Weighs how well you know each connector and how well they know the person, rather than giving a list of people you both know.

title: The best introducer, with /intro
when: You know who you want to meet and want someone who can introduce you, in one command.
prompt: /intro What is the best person to introduce me to @[person]?
why: The /intro command tells O to look for someone who can introduce you, so you get the one person to ask, not a list of people you both know.

title: Who in my network can vouch for me at this company
when: You are pitching a company and want a reference they trust.
prompt: I'm pitching @[company]. Who in my network has worked there, sold to them, or sits on their board, and who among them would vouch for me?
why: Finds the people they already trust who also know you.

title: Find a board member
when: You have a board seat to fill and know the kind of person you want.
prompt: Who in my network could sit on the board of [company], given we need [experience]? Rank by fit, independence and how well I know them.
why: Searches your own network for people who fit the board role, and checks how independent each one is.

title: Find candidates in my network for a role
when: You have a role to fill and want to look before it goes to a recruiter.
prompt: I'm hiring a [role]. Who in my network fits, or is one introduction away from someone who does? Give me the top [10] with why, and who could make the intro.
why: Includes people one introduction away, and names who can introduce you to each candidate.

title: Find design partners or first customers
when: You have a product that needs its first ten conversations.
prompt: Who in my network runs or influences [function] at companies with [criteria]? I'm looking for design partners for [product]. Top [15], with the angle for each.
why: Matches people on their role, the kind of company they work at, and how you know them.

title: Investors in a place, at a stage
when: You're raising money locally, or travelling.
prompt: Show me investors in [city] in my network who write [pre-seed / seed] cheques and are active this year. Top [10], with how I know them.
why: Picks investors who are actually active, not just anyone with the word investor in their headline.

title: Who do I know at this company
when: The simplest question, asked often.
prompt: Who do I know at @[company], and who there previously worked at @[other company]?
why: Who is there now and where they worked before, in one answer, with the overlap you asked for.

title: Experts on a topic in a place
when: You need someone who really knows the subject.
prompt: Who are the most senior people in my network working on [topic] in [place]? Rank by depth of expertise and how well I know them.
why: Judges how deep someone's knowledge goes from their career and their work, not from keywords.

title: The most seasoned people in my network
when: You want the people who have done it more than once.
prompt: Who are the most seasoned [entrepreneurs / operators] in my network: people who have built more than one company that ran for at least three years?
why: Counts what people have actually done across their whole career.

title: Who did I connect with, and what does it say
when: Every couple of weeks.
prompt: Who did I connect with in the past two weeks? Give me a table with their industries and companies, and tell me what pattern you see.
why: A table, plus what it tells you as a whole.

title: Who should I introduce to each other
when: You want to be useful to the people you know.
prompt: Inside my @[circle], who are the five pairs of people I should introduce to each other, where their backgrounds fill gaps in each other's work?
why: Finds pairs whose backgrounds fill each other's gaps, with the reason to make each introduction.

title: Who did I meet at that event
when: Months later, there's a name you can't place.
prompt: Who did I meet at [event] on [dates]? What did we talk about, and did anything come of it?
why: Puts your calendar, messages and the dates you connected into one answer.

title: Prepare my week
when: Monday morning.
prompt: Help me prepare for the week ahead. Go through my emails, calendar and messages: what is coming, who do I need to get back to, and where should I spend my attention?
why: A plan built from your own email, calendar and messages, not a to-do list you typed.

title: Where my network is thin
when: You're planning which relationships to work on over the next three months.
prompt: Given what I'm building at [company], where is my network strong and where is it thin? Who are the ten people I should establish a relationship with, and who can get me to each?
why: Shows where your network falls short of your goal, and how to reach the people who would fill the gap.

title: Set a reminder on a relationship
when: You promised to follow up.
prompt: Remind me [tomorrow at 16:00] to reach out to @[person] about [topic].
why: The reminder is attached to the relationship, so you get the background with it when it comes up.
